functions.yields: Adjusted R² as a scalar, typically in [0, 1] but can be negative
functions.description:
Adjusted R² penalises R² for the number of predictors relative to sample size, correcting for the inflation that occurs when irrelevant predictors are added. It equals 1 - (1 - R²) × df_total / df_residual, which reduces to the familiar 1 - (1 - R²)(n-1)/(n-k-1) when an intercept is fit. Unlike R² it can decrease when a predictor adds less explanatory power than expected by chance, and can be negative when the model fits worse than a horizontal line.

Computed as 1 - (1 - R_Squared(...)) * Total_Degrees_Of_Freedom(...) / Residual_Degrees_Of_Freedom(...), inheriting the Allow_Intercept correction from both df functions.
functions.plain_language_summary: R-squared adjusted so extra predictors do not get free credit.
functions.notes: R² penalised for model complexity: 1 − (1 − R²)·df_total/df_residual. Can be negative when the model fits worse than the mean.

functions.yields: PRESS (Prediction Residual Error Sum of Squares) as a scalar
functions.description:
PRESS is the leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) sum of squared prediction errors. For each observation i the model is refitted on all other observations and evaluated at x_i; the shortcut formula avoids n separate refits by computing Σ(eᵢ / (1 − hᵢ))² where eᵢ are the OLS residuals and hᵢ are the hat-matrix diagonal (leverage) values.

Computed as SUMSQ(LOOCV_Residual(...)), where LOOCV_Residual returns eᵢ / (1 − hᵢ) using Residuals() and Hat_Diagonal().

functions.notes: Leave-one-out cross-validation sum of squares = Σ(eᵢ/(1−hᵢ))². Lower values mean better out-of-sample predictions.

functions.yields: Durbin-Watson statistic as a scalar
functions.description:
DW = Σ(eₜ − eₜ₋₁)² / Σeₜ², testing for first-order serial correlation in residuals. Values near 2 indicate no autocorrelation; values below ~1.5 suggest positive autocorrelation, values above ~2.5 suggest negative autocorrelation.

Computed as SUM((DROP(e,1) − DROP(e,−1))²) / SUM(e²), where DROP(e,1) removes the first residual (giving e₂..eₙ) and DROP(e,−1) removes the last (giving e₁..eₙ₋₁), so consecutive differences are formed without OFFSET or index arithmetic.
functions.plain_language_summary: Whether nearby residuals tend to move together instead of staying independent.
functions.notes: Test statistic for first-order serial autocorrelation in residuals. Values near 2 = no autocorrelation; < 1.5 or > 2.5 flag problems.

functions.description:
Standardized (Beta) coefficient for predictor j = b_j × std(X_j) / std(Y). Expresses each coefficient in standard-deviation units, making predictors with different scales directly comparable in magnitude. Always returns k values (one per predictor); the intercept has no meaningful standardized counterpart and is excluded.

functions.yields: k×1 column vector of VIF values, one per predictor (does not include an intercept row)
functions.description:
Variance Inflation Factor for each predictor Xⱼ = 1 / (1 − R²ⱼ), where R²ⱼ is the R² from regressing Xⱼ on all other predictors. VIF measures how much the variance of coefficient j is inflated by multicollinearity. VIF = 1 means no collinearity; VIF > 10 (or > 5 by stricter convention) signals a problem.

Auxiliary regressions always include an intercept regardless of the main model's Allow_Intercept setting (standard convention). When k = 1 the function returns 1 (no collinearity possible with a single predictor). Uses MAKEARRAY + FILTER to iterate over column indices without VBA or helper columns.
functions.plain_language_summary: How much overlap with other predictors is inflating each coefficient's instability.
functions.notes: Variance Inflation Factor per predictor = 1/(1−R²ⱼ). VIF = 1: no collinearity. VIF > 5: review. VIF > 10: problem.

functions.notes: 1/VIF per predictor. Fraction of unique variance not shared with other predictors. < 0.2: review; < 0.1: strong collinearity.

functions.name: Prediction_Interval
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(X_s, Y, X_new, [Allow_Intercept], [Include], [alpha],
  LET(
    allow_arg,     IF(ISOMITTED(Allow_Intercept), TRUE, Allow_Intercept),
    filt_arg,      IF(ISOMITTED(Include),          TRUE, Include),
    alpha_arg,     IF(ISOMITTED(alpha),           0.05, alpha),
    X_design,      Design_Matrix(X_s, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    beta,          Coefficients(X_s, Y, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    s,             SE_Regression(X_s, Y, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    df,            Residual_Degrees_Of_Freedom(X_s, Y, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    t_crit,        T.INV.2T(alpha_arg, df),
    x_new_aligned, IF(allow_arg, X_new, INDEX(X_new, SEQUENCE(ROWS(X_new) - 1, 1, 2, 1))),
    XtX_inv,       Gram_Inverse(X_design),
    h_new,         MMULT(MMULT(TRANSPOSE(x_new_aligned), XtX_inv), x_new_aligned),
    point_est,     SUMPRODUCT(x_new_aligned, beta),
    se_pred,       s * SQRT(1 + h_new),
    margin,        t_crit * se_pred,
    VSTACK(
      point_est,
      se_pred,
      t_crit,
      point_est - margin,
      point_est + margin,
      1 - alpha_arg
    )
  ))

functions.name: Exclude_Row_N
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(array, n,
  LET(
    total_rows, ROWS(array),
    n_abs,      IF(n < 0, total_rows + n + 1, n),
    IF(
      OR(n_abs < 1, n_abs > total_rows),
      NA(),
      LET(
        rows, SEQUENCE(total_rows),
        CHOOSEROWS(array, FILTER(rows, rows <> n_abs))

    )
  )
)

functions.yields: k×1 column vector of Pearson correlations between each predictor and Y
functions.description:
Pearson_R computes the linear (Pearson product-moment) correlation between each column of X_s and Y after applying the optional Include argument. When X_s has a single column the result is a scalar; when X_s has k columns it spills as a k×1 column vector.

A Pearson_R close to ±1 indicates a strong linear association. Comparing Pearson_R with Spearman_R on the same data reveals nonlinearity: a large gap (Spearman > Pearson in magnitude) suggests a monotonic but curved relationship that may warrant a log or polynomial transformation.
functions.plain_language_summary: The straight-line relationship between each predictor and the outcome.
functions.notes: Linear (Pearson) correlations between each X_s column and Y. Returns a k×1 vector. Compare with Spearman_R to detect nonlinearity.

functions.name: Spearman_R
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(xf, yf, [Include],
  LET(
    baseFilter, IF(ISOMITTED(Include), TRUE, Include),
    RankAvgAsc, LAMBDA(a,
      MAP(a, LAMBDA(v, 1+SUM(--(a<v))+(SUM(--(a=v))-1)/2))
    ),
    TRANSPOSE(
      BYCOL(xf,
        LAMBDA(xcol,
          LET(
            valid, baseFilter*ISNUMBER(xcol)*ISNUMBER(yf),
            x, FILTER(xcol, valid),
            y, FILTER(yf, valid),
            rx, RankAvgAsc(x),
            ry, RankAvgAsc(y),
            CORREL(rx, ry)
          )
        )
      )
    )
  ))

arguments.description: predictor column range (single or multi-column); returns one correlation per column

arguments.description: single-column outcome range

arguments.name: Include
arguments.description: boolean array — TRUE includes the row, FALSE excludes it

functions.yields: k×1 column vector of Spearman rank correlations between each predictor and Y
functions.description:
Spearman_R computes the rank (Spearman) correlation between each column of xf and yf. For each predictor column, rows are kept where both that column and yf are numeric (and pass the optional Include). Ties receive average ranks via a MAP-based helper (avoids RANK.AVG on dynamic arrays). Returns a k×1 vector when xf has k columns.

Unlike Pearson_R, Spearman_R measures any monotonic relationship, not just linear ones. The diagnostic value of the pair is in their difference: if |Spearman_R| is noticeably larger than |Pearson_R| for the same predictor, the relationship is curved and a transformation (e.g. LOG) or a nonlinear term may improve model fit.

functions.notes: Rank (Spearman) correlations between each X_s column and Y. Detects monotonic but curved relationships. Returns a k×1 vector.

functions.description:
F_Statistic returns the F-statistic for the omnibus test of the null hypothesis that all regression coefficients are simultaneously zero. It equals (MS_Regression / MS_Residual) = (SS_Regression / df_regression) / (SS_Residual / df_residual).

A large F-statistic (and correspondingly small F_Statistic_P_Value) means the model explains significantly more variance than would be expected by chance. Note that a significant F does not guarantee that every individual predictor is significant — individual t-statistics (T_Statistics) address that question. F_Statistic appears in the ANOVA table on the Regression sheet; this function exposes it as a named reference for use in other formulas.
functions.plain_language_summary: Whether the model, taken as a whole, explains more than random noise would.
functions.notes: Overall F-statistic = MS_Regression / MS_Residual. Tests whether the model explains significantly more variance than random noise.

Use this to screen for multicollinearity before fitting a model: pairs with |r| > 0.7 are candidates for VIF investigation. functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),

  ))

arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count via Sturges' rule
functions.description:
Sturges_Bins returns the bin count k = ⌈log₂(n) + 1⌉, where n is the count of numeric values after filtering. Sturges' rule works well for roughly symmetric, unimodal data with moderate sample sizes (50–200 observations). It tends to undersmooth (too few bins) for skewed or heavy-tailed data.

Used by Bin_Edges to generate upper bin edges for the Sturges histogram column chart.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins Sturges' rule recommends for this data.
functions.notes: Bin count k = ⌈log₂(n)+1⌉ (Sturges’ rule). Reliable for roughly symmetric data with 50–200 observations.

functions.name: Scott_Bins
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),
    sd, STDEV.S(x),
    width, 3.49 * sd * n ^ (-1/3),
    range_, MAX(x) - MIN(x),
    IF(sd = 0, 1, CEILING(range_ / width, 1))
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count via Scott's normal reference rule
functions.description:
Scott_Bins computes the bin width h = 3.49 × σ × n^(−1/3) that minimises mean integrated squared error assuming the data are normally distributed, then returns k = ⌈range / h⌉.

Scott's rule is more adaptive than Sturges for larger samples and performs well when the data are approximately normal. For strongly skewed or multimodal data, Freedman-Diaconis is more appropriate.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins Scott's normal-reference rule recommends.
functions.notes: Bin count from Scott’s normal-reference rule: width = 3.49·σ·n^(−1/3). Optimal when data are approximately normal.

functions.name: Freedman_Diaconis_Bins
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),
    iqr, QUARTILE.EXC(x, 3) - QUARTILE.EXC(x, 1),
    width, 2 * iqr * n ^ (-1/3),
    range_, MAX(x) - MIN(x),
    IF(iqr = 0, Sturges_Bins(data, filt_arg), CEILING(range_ / width, 1))
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count via the Freedman-Diaconis rule
functions.description:
Freedman_Diaconis_Bins computes the bin width h = 2 × IQR × n^(−1/3) where IQR is the interquartile range (QUARTILE.EXC), then returns k = ⌈range / h⌉.

Freedman-Diaconis is robust to outliers because it uses the IQR rather than the standard deviation. It is the preferred rule for skewed or heavy-tailed distributions and for large samples where the shape deviates from normality.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins the Freedman-Diaconis rule recommends.
functions.notes: Bin count from Freedman-Diaconis rule: width = 2·IQR·n^(−1/3). Robust to outliers; preferred for skewed data.

functions.name: Number_Of_Histogram_Bins
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [method], [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),
    m, IF(ISOMITTED(method), "FD", method),
    SWITCH(m,
      "Sturges", CEILING(LOG(n, 2) + 1, 1),
      "Scott",   LET(
                   sd, STDEV.S(x),
                   range_, MAX(x) - MIN(x),
                   IF(sd = 0, 1, CEILING(range_ / (3.49 * sd * n ^ (-1/3)), 1))
                 ),
      LET(
        iqr, QUARTILE.EXC(x, 3) - QUARTILE.EXC(x, 1),
        range_, MAX(x) - MIN(x),
        IF(iqr = 0,
          CEILING(LOG(n, 2) + 1, 1),
          CEILING(range_ / (2 * iqr * n ^ (-1/3)), 1))
      )
    )
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: bin-count rule: "Sturges", "Scott", or "FD" (default when omitted)

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count k for the chosen method
functions.description:
Number_Of_Histogram_Bins returns the recommended number of histogram bins k using the specified rule, defaulting to Freedman-Diaconis when method is omitted.

All three methods are computed inline without calling other named LAMBDAs:
  Sturges: k = ⌈log₂(n) + 1⌉
  Scott:   width = 3.49 × SD × n^(−1/3);  k = ⌈range / width⌉  (k=1 when SD=0)
  FD:      width = 2 × IQR × n^(−1/3);   k = ⌈range / width⌉  (falls back to Sturges when IQR=0)

Used internally by Bin_Edges. Can also be called directly to get the bin count for a specific rule.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins a chosen rule (default: Freedman-Diaconis) recommends for this data.
functions.notes: Bin count by chosen rule ("Sturges", "Scott", or default "FD"). Used internally by Bin_Edges; call directly to inspect the count.

functions.name: Bin_Edges
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [method], [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    min_x, MIN(x),
    max_x, MAX(x),
    k, Number_Of_Histogram_Bins(data, IF(ISOMITTED(method), "FD", method), filt_arg),
    width, (max_x - min_x) / k,
    SEQUENCE(k + 1, 1, min_x, width)
  ))

The vector is computed as SEQUENCE(k+1, 1, min, width), so every boundary is evenly spaced by width = (max - min) / k. =LAMBDA(maximum, min_val, mode_val, max_val, [minimum],
  LET(
    cdf_at, LAMBDA(x,
      IFERROR(IF(x < min_val, 0,
        IF(x < mode_val,

    cdf_min, IF(ISOMITTED(minimum), 0,
      LET(z_min, (minimum - min_val) / (max_val - min_val + 1E-30),

Grid_Argument_Minimum finds the minimum numeric value in a rectangular grid and returns that value together with its 1-based row and column locations. TOCOL scans the grid by row, XMATCH selects the first occurrence of the minimum, and QUOTIENT/MOD convert the flattened position back to grid coordinates. Returning one matched position avoids combining the row of one tied minimum with the column of another.

For a two-input Excel Data Table, pass only the Data Table body, excluding the parameter headings, parameter-value axes, and corner formula cell. The grid is expected to contain numeric results; an all-nonnumeric grid returns NA() in all three output positions.

functions.name: NLL_Triangular
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, min_val, mode_val, max_val, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    range_, max_val - min_val,
    pdf, IF(
      x <= mode_val,
      2 * (x - min_val)  / (range_ * (mode_val - min_val)),
      2 * (max_val - x)  / (range_ * (max_val - mode_val))
    ),
    IFERROR(-SUMPRODUCT(LN(pdf)), 1E+15)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column data range

arguments.name: min_val
arguments.description: lower bound of the triangular distribution

arguments.name: mode_val
arguments.description: peak (most likely value)

arguments.name: max_val
arguments.description: upper bound

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array; defaults to ISNUMBER(data)

functions.yields: negative log-likelihood for Triangular(min, mode, max) given data; returns 1E+15 for invalid parameters
functions.description:
NLL_Triangular implements the triangular PDF directly: 2(x − min) / (range × (mode − min)) on [min, mode] and 2(max − x) / (range × (max − mode)) on (mode, max]. The likelihood is non-differentiable at the mode, so MLE is non-standard; the conventional approach is to set min = data min, mode = data mode, max = data max.

Triangular is common in project risk and cost estimation (three-point estimates). Pass to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 3.
functions.plain_language_summary: How unlikely the Triangular distribution is to have generated this data at the given bounds.
functions.notes: Negative log-likelihood for Triangular(min, mode, max). Conventional MLE: set min, mode, max to the data min, mode, and max.

functions.description:
NLL_Beta evaluates −Σ ln f(xᵢ | α, β) via BETA.DIST. Values exactly at 0 or 1 cause BETA.DIST to return errors; the IFERROR sentinel catches these and maps the entire NLL to 1E+15, making the cell visible as an overflow region in grid-search heatmaps.

Beta fits proportions and rates bounded on [0, 1] (e.g. efficiencies, fractions). Data must be rescaled to (0, 1) before fitting. No closed-form MLE; fit using grid-search Data Table (v2.1). Pass to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 2.

functions.notes: Negative log-likelihood for Beta(alpha, beta). Data must be strictly on (0, 1). No closed-form MLE; use a grid-search Data Table.

functions.name: NLL_BetaPERT
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, min_val, mode_val, max_val, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    range_, max_val - min_val,
    z, (x - min_val) / range_,
    alpha_p, 1 + 4 * (mode_val - min_val) / range_,
    beta_p,  1 + 4 * (max_val  - mode_val) / range_,
    pdf_z, BETA.DIST(z, alpha_p, beta_p, FALSE),
    pdf_x, pdf_z / range_,
    IFERROR(-SUMPRODUCT(LN(pdf_x)), 1E+15)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column data range

arguments.name: min_val
arguments.description: lower bound (minimum possible value)

arguments.name: mode_val
arguments.description: most likely value (peak of the PERT curve)

arguments.name: max_val
arguments.description: upper bound (maximum possible value)

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array; defaults to ISNUMBER(data)

functions.yields: negative log-likelihood for BetaPERT(min, mode, max) given data; returns 1E+15 for invalid parameters
functions.description:
NLL_BetaPERT reparameterises the Beta distribution using the PERT convention: α = 1 + 4·(mode − min)/(max − min), β = 1 + 4·(max − mode)/(max − min). Data are rescaled to z = (x − min)/(max − min); the Jacobian correction log(1/(max − min)) converts the Beta log-likelihood back to the original data scale.

BetaPERT is the standard distribution for three-point cost and schedule estimates. Parameters are estimated directly from min, mode, max; no optimisation is needed. Pass to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 3.

functions.notes: Negative log-likelihood for BetaPERT(min, mode, max). Parameters come from three-point estimates; no optimisation needed.

functions.name: GoF_AIC
functions.formula_display: =LAMBDA(nll, k, 2 * k + 2 * nll)

arguments.name: nll
arguments.description: negative log-likelihood from any NLL_* function

arguments.name: k
arguments.description: number of free parameters in the distribution (1 for Exponential, 2 for Normal/Lognormal/Weibull/Gamma/Beta, 3 for Triangular/BetaPERT)

functions.yields: AIC = 2k + 2·NLL as a scalar
functions.description:
GoF_AIC computes the Akaike Information Criterion: AIC = 2k + 2·NLL. Lower AIC indicates a better balance of fit quality and model complexity. AIC is comparable across all distributions fitted to the same dataset — the distribution with the lowest AIC is the best-fitting model under this criterion.

AIC does not penalise extra parameters as strongly as BIC, so it may favour more complex distributions (larger k) when sample sizes are large. For small samples, use AICc instead (not implemented here — add a correction term 2k(k+1)/(n−k−1) if n/k < 40).
functions.plain_language_summary: A model-comparison score that balances fit quality against the number of parameters.
functions.notes: AIC = 2k + 2·NLL for distribution comparison. k = number of free parameters. Lower = better. Compare across distributions on same data.

functions.name: GoF_BIC
functions.formula_display: =LAMBDA(nll, k, n, k * LN(n) + 2 * nll)

arguments.name: nll
arguments.description: negative log-likelihood from any NLL_* function

arguments.name: k
arguments.description: number of free parameters in the distribution

arguments.name: n
arguments.description: number of observations used in the fit (from UV_n or COUNT(data))

functions.yields: BIC = k·ln(n) + 2·NLL as a scalar
functions.description:
GoF_BIC computes the Bayesian Information Criterion: BIC = k·ln(n) + 2·NLL. Lower BIC indicates a better model. BIC penalises extra parameters more strongly than AIC (penalty grows with log(n) rather than 2), favouring simpler distributions in larger samples.

Compare AIC and BIC together: if they agree, the best-fit distribution is clear; if they disagree, AIC is selecting a more complex distribution and BIC is selecting a simpler one. The difference is informative about how much the extra parameters contribute to fit.
functions.plain_language_summary: A model-comparison score that penalises extra parameters more strongly as sample size grows.
functions.notes: BIC = k·ln(n) + 2·NLL. Penalises extra parameters more than AIC (penalty scales with log n). Lower = better.

functions.name: GoF_Anderson_Darling
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, dist_cdf, [include],
  LET(
    inc, IF(ISOMITTED(include), ISNUMBER(data), include),
    d, FILTER(data, inc),
    f, FILTER(dist_cdf, inc),
    n, ROWS(d),
    IF(n = 0, NA(),
    LET(
      fs, SORTBY(f, d),
      eps, 1E-10,
      fc, IF(fs < eps, eps, IF(fs > 1 - eps, 1 - eps, fs)),
      i, SEQUENCE(n),
      fc_rev, SORTBY(fc, i, -1),
      -n - SUMPRODUCT((2 * i - 1) * (LN(fc) + LN(1 - fc_rev))) / n
    ))
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column data range

arguments.name: dist_cdf
arguments.description: CDF values evaluated at each data point under the fitted distribution (same size as data; e.g. NORM.DIST(data, mean, sd, TRUE))

arguments.name: include
arguments.description: optional boolean array — TRUE keeps the row, FALSE excludes it; defaults to ISNUMBER(data)

functions.yields: Anderson-Darling A² statistic as a scalar (lower = better fit)
functions.description:
GoF_Anderson_Darling computes the Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit statistic: A² = −n − (1/n) Σᵢ (2i−1)·[ln F(X₍ᵢ₎) + ln(1 − F(X₍ₙ₊₁₋ᵢ₎))]. CDF values are sorted by data internally. An epsilon clamp (1E-10) prevents ln(0) for bounded-support distributions (Beta, Triangular, BetaPERT) whose CDF can reach exactly 0 or 1 at support edges.

A-D is more sensitive to tail deviations than K-S, making it better at detecting departures in the extremes. Lower A² indicates a better fit. Compare alongside AIC, BIC, and K-S in the fit comparison table.
functions.plain_language_summary: Anderson-Darling A² = −n − (1/n)·Σ(2i−1)[ln F(xᵢ) + ln(1−F(x_{n+1−i}))] (lower = better fit).
functions.notes: Anderson-Darling A² goodness-of-fit. More sensitive to tail deviations than K-S. Lower = better. Compare with AIC, BIC, and K-S.

functions.name: GoF_Kolmogorov_Smirnov
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, dist_cdf, [include],
  LET(
    inc, IF(ISOMITTED(include), ISNUMBER(data), include),
    d, FILTER(data, inc),
    f, FILTER(dist_cdf, inc),
    n, ROWS(d),
    IF(n = 0, NA(),
    LET(
      fs, SORTBY(f, d),
      i, SEQUENCE(n),
      d_plus, MAX(i / n - fs),
      d_minus, MAX(fs - (i - 1) / n),
      MAX(d_plus, d_minus)
    ))
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column data range

arguments.name: dist_cdf
arguments.description: CDF values evaluated at each data point under the fitted distribution (same size as data; e.g. NORM.DIST(data, mean, sd, TRUE))

arguments.name: include
arguments.description: optional boolean array — TRUE keeps the row, FALSE excludes it; defaults to ISNUMBER(data)

functions.yields: Kolmogorov-Smirnov D statistic as a scalar in [0, 1] (lower = better fit)
functions.description:
GoF_Kolmogorov_Smirnov computes the Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit statistic: D = max(D⁺, D⁻) where D⁺ = maxᵢ(i/n − F(X₍ᵢ₎)) and D⁻ = maxᵢ(F(X₍ᵢ₎) − (i−1)/n). This is the maximum vertical distance between the empirical CDF and the fitted CDF.

K-S is sensitive to the single largest deviation between the empirical and fitted distributions, making it complementary to A-D (which weights tails more heavily). Lower D indicates a better fit. D is bounded on [0, 1]; values near 0 mean the fitted CDF closely tracks the empirical CDF.
functions.plain_language_summary: Kolmogorov-Smirnov D = max|F_n(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ)| (lower = better fit).
functions.notes: Kolmogorov-Smirnov D = max|F_n(xᵢ) − F(xᵢ)|. Maximum deviation between empirical and fitted CDFs. Lower = better.

functions.name: Dummy_Levels
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(category, [reference], [include],
    LET(
        inc,        IF(ISOMITTED(include), TRUE, include),
        x,          TOCOL(IF(category = "", "", category), 0),
        active,     (x<>"") * inc,
        x_active,   FILTER(x, active, NA()),
        All_Levels, IFERROR(TOROW(SORT(UNIQUE(x_active))), NA()),
        ref_given,  NOT(ISOMITTED(reference)),
        ref,        IF(ref_given, reference, IFERROR(INDEX(All_Levels, 1, 1), NA())),
        ref_ok,     IFERROR(ISNUMBER(MATCH(ref, All_Levels, 0)), FALSE),
        IF(OR(ISNA(All_Levels), NOT(ref_ok)),
           NA(),
           IFERROR(FILTER(All_Levels, All_Levels <> ref), NA())
        )
    )
)

arguments.name: category
arguments.description: single-column categorical data range

arguments.name: reference
arguments.description: the level to drop (treatment coding); when omitted, the first sorted level is dropped

arguments.name: include
arguments.description: boolean mask — TRUE keeps the row; when omitted all non-blank rows are used

functions.yields: 1 × k horizontal vector of retained category labels (sorted, reference level removed); #N/A on degenerate input
functions.description:
Dummy_Levels returns the set of category labels that will become dummy columns after treatment coding. It sorts all levels present in the included sample, drops the reference level, and returns the remainder as a horizontal row vector.

When reference is omitted, the first sorted level is used as the reference (alphabetically first). When reference is supplied, it is validated against the included sample; if not found, the function returns #N/A rather than silently failing to drop a column.

Use Dummy_Levels as a header row above Dummy_Code to label dummy columns, or to inspect which levels the model will contain before fitting.

Truly empty cells are normalized to "" before the row mask is applied, so a blank category cell is excluded rather than coerced to a spurious numeric-zero level; genuine 0 values pass through untouched.

Failure is signaled by type, not by text: degenerate inputs return a genuine Excel error (#N/A via NA()) that every downstream IFERROR/ISNA guard can catch, never a descriptive string that would silently participate in array math. The three failure conditions — an included sample with no non-blank category values, a reference level not present in the included sample, and a sample containing only one level (nothing left to code after the reference is dropped) — all return #N/A. The human-readable explanation is carried by the consuming sheet's conditional formatting, not by the return value.
functions.plain_language_summary: The k category labels that become dummy columns (sorted, reference level removed).
functions.notes: Retained category labels after treatment coding: sorted levels from the included sample with the reference level dropped. Use as a header row above the Dummy_Code matrix. Returns #N/A (a real Excel error, catchable by ISNA/IFERROR) on degenerate input.

Dummy_Code returns a treatment-coded dummy matrix for a categorical variable. For each included row, the value is compared to each retained level and encoded as 1 (match) or 0 (no match). Excluded rows (include = FALSE or blank category value) return "" across all k columns so the spilled array stays row-aligned with the source data.

Level determination is delegated to Dummy_Levels — one source of truth for which levels are retained — so the two functions can never disagree about the level set. The reference level is dropped to avoid perfect multicollinearity when the design includes an intercept. Reference-level validation is enforced: if the supplied reference does not appear in the included sample, the function returns #N/A rather than silently failing to drop a column — an invalid reference reintroduces the exact collinearity the function exists to prevent.

Pair with Dummy_Levels to get the matching column headers. Pass the output directly to HSTACK to assemble a multi-predictor design for Coefficients, Prediction_Interval, and related functions.

Failure is signaled by type, not by text: degenerate inputs return a genuine Excel error (#N/A via NA()) that every downstream IFERROR/ISNA guard can catch, never a descriptive string that would silently participate in array math. The three failure conditions — an included sample with no non-blank category values, a reference level not present in the included sample, and a sample containing only one level (nothing left to code after the reference is dropped) — all return #N/A.
functions.plain_language_summary: Treatment-coded dummy matrix for a categorical predictor, with excluded rows as blank and the reference level dropped.
functions.notes: Treatment-coded 0/1 dummy matrix, row-aligned to the source data. Levels come from Dummy_Levels (one source of truth); the reference level is dropped to avoid collinearity with the intercept; excluded rows return "". Returns #N/A on degenerate input.

regression_sheet_notes.Pearson R: Measures the straight-line relationship between a predictor and Y. Values near 1 or -1 mean a strong linear relationship; values near 0 mean little linear pattern.
regression_sheet_notes.Spearman R: Measures whether higher X tends to go with higher or lower Y after converting both to ranks. It is useful when the relationship is ordered but curved instead of perfectly linear.
regression_sheet_notes.Skewness: Shows whether the data have a longer tail on one side. Positive means a longer right tail; negative means a longer left tail.
regression_sheet_notes.Kurtosis: Shows how heavy the tails are relative to a normal bell curve. Positive values mean heavier tails with more frequent extremes; values near 0 match a normal distribution.
regression_sheet_notes.VIF: A measure of collinearity with the other predictors. A value of 1 means no overlap; above 5 warrants review, above 10 indicates a problem.
regression_sheet_notes.Tolerance: The fraction of a predictor's variation not explained by the other predictors. Values below 0.2 warrant review; below 0.1 indicate strong collinearity.
regression_sheet_notes.Multiple R: How closely the model's predicted Y values track the actual Y values overall.
regression_sheet_notes.R Square: The share of the outcome's variation explained by the model.
regression_sheet_notes.Adjusted R Square: R Square with a penalty for adding predictors that do not help enough.
regression_sheet_notes.Standard Error: The typical size of the model's prediction errors, measured in the same units as Y.
regression_sheet_notes.Observations: The number of rows actually used in the regression after filtering.
regression_sheet_notes.PRESS: A leave-one-out prediction error score. Lower is better because it means the model predicts unseen rows more accurately.
regression_sheet_notes.PRESS R²: An out-of-sample version of R Square based on leave-one-out prediction. Negative values mean the model predicts worse than just using the average Y.
regression_sheet_notes.Mean Leverage: The average influence each row exerts on the fitted line based on how far it sits from the center of the predictor space. Rows above 2× or 3× this value are flagged by the conditional formatting.
regression_sheet_notes.AIC: A model-comparison score that balances fit against complexity. Lower is better when comparing models on the same data.
regression_sheet_notes.BIC: Another model-comparison score like AIC, but it penalizes extra predictors more strongly.
regression_sheet_notes.AICc: AIC with an extra correction for small samples.
regression_sheet_notes.QQ Correlation: A numeric check of how close the residuals are to a normal bell shape. Values closer to 1 are better.
regression_sheet_notes.Alpha: The cutoff for statistical significance. At 0.05, results with p-values below 0.05 are treated as statistically significant.
regression_sheet_notes.df: The number of independent data points available to estimate each part of the model — total rows minus one for each estimated parameter.
regression_sheet_notes.SS: The total variation attributed to that source — regression, residual, or total. The raw material from which MS and F are calculated.
regression_sheet_notes.MS: Sum of squares averaged over its degrees of freedom — a per-unit measure of variation for that source.
regression_sheet_notes.F: The model-vs-noise ratio used in the overall regression significance test.
regression_sheet_notes.Significance F: The p-value for the overall F test. Small values mean the model as a whole is unlikely to be pure noise.
regression_sheet_notes.Regression: The variation explained by the predictors taken together.
regression_sheet_notes.Residual: The variation the model does not explain.
regression_sheet_notes.Total: All variation in the outcome before splitting it into explained and unexplained parts.
regression_sheet_notes.Coefficients: The fitted weights used to turn predictor values into predictions.
regression_sheet_notes.Std Error: How uncertain each coefficient estimate is.
regression_sheet_notes.t Stat: How many standard errors the coefficient is away from zero.
regression_sheet_notes.P-value: How surprising this coefficient would be if its true effect were zero. Smaller values mean stronger evidence of a real effect.
regression_sheet_notes.Lower 95%: The lower bound of the 95% confidence interval.
regression_sheet_notes.Upper 95%: The upper bound of the 95% confidence interval.
regression_sheet_notes.Beta Weight: The coefficient after standardizing units, so predictors can be compared on the same scale.
regression_sheet_notes.Point Estimate: The model's single best predicted Y value for the inputs you entered.
regression_sheet_notes.SE Prediction: The standard error for a new prediction. It reflects both model uncertainty and ordinary row-to-row noise.
regression_sheet_notes.t Critical: The t-distribution cutoff at the chosen confidence level. Multiply by SE Prediction to get the prediction interval half-width.
regression_sheet_notes.Confidence Level: The probability level associated with the interval. With alpha 0.05, this is 95%.
regression_sheet_notes.Predicted Y: The fitted outcome values produced by the model.
regression_sheet_notes.Residuals: Actual Y minus predicted Y. Positive means the row came in above the model's prediction; negative means below.
regression_sheet_notes.LOOCV Residual: The prediction error for a row when that row is left out of the fitting step.
regression_sheet_notes.Hat Diagonal: Leverage. It shows how unusual a row's predictor values are relative to the rest of the data.
regression_sheet_notes.Studentized Residuals: Residuals scaled to account for overall error size and leverage, making outliers easier to compare fairly.
regression_sheet_notes.Cook's Distance: How much a single row can pull the fitted coefficients and predictions around.
regression_sheet_notes.Normal Scores Ranked: Expected bell-curve quantiles used for the Q-Q comparison.
regression_sheet_notes.Studentized Residuals Ranked: Studentized residuals sorted from smallest to largest for the Q-Q plot.
regression_sheet_notes.Scale-Location: The square root of the absolute studentized residual. A flat pattern suggests stable error spread.
regression_sheet_notes.PRESS Residual: A leverage-adjusted residual used to show how much a row affects out-of-sample prediction error.
